pr_title: fixed some triangles not being found in Octree due to small floating point inaccuracies
pr_body:
Fixed: #21755 
Due to small floating point inaccuracies in the order of one millionth of a millimeter, in practice some triangles would not be found for some of the subtrees. This could result moving through faces of Axis Aligned 3d objects. To fix this, make each subtree slightly larger to make sure that all relevant triangles are found.
pr_comments:
>in practice some triangles would not be found for some of the subtrees.

Can you provide a simple example to demonstrate the issue?

And where in the code is the test failing?

Assuming the floating point issues can't be avoided when calculating new bounds extents a fixed epsilon isn't a good solution because the maximum amount of possible floating point error grows with the size of the number.

For [three-mesh-bvh](https://github.com/gkjohnson/three-mesh-bvh) the max amount of floating point error for a given number is computed using the [machine epsilon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_epsilon#Values_for_standard_hardware_floating_point_arithmetics) value for 32 bit floating point values (2e-24) which is used to avoid similar issues when computing bounds extents. I think the same thing could be done here but I agree it would be helpful if a demonstration of the issue were provided.

@SnoekJim  Let's continue the discussion in #21755 by answering https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/pull/21756#issuecomment-831277203.

The PR in its current form can't be merged.

issue_context.title: Octree - sometimes some triangles will not be found for some of the subtrees
issue_context.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

Using octree, it is sometimes possible to move through faces of Axis Aligned 3d objects such as a wall.
Due to small floating point inaccuracies in the order of one millionth of a millimeter, in practice some triangles would not be found for some of the subtrees.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

To fix this, make each subtree slightly larger to make sure that all relevant triangles are found.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

There are no alternative solutions we've considered.

**Additional context**

The project we're working on aims to let customers experience their buildings in 3d using first person controls.
comments: Please provide a simple example to demonstrate the issue.
Yes, I will try to provide an example, hopefully as soon as tomorrow. Otherwise it will be later this week

While working at #21834, I've noticed that the collision detection in `games_fps` is not very reliable. With a low framerate (e.g. 30 fps) it only takes a few tries and the player can pass the walls of the round tower in the middle of the map. It's also possible to glitch through the entire map. With a higher framerate, this problem is less visible though.

I assume that happens because of larger time delta values and thus larger translations of the player (especially with a high velocity). This results in situations where the players "passes through obstacles" because in one frame the player's bounding volume is before a triangle and in the next frame completely behind it. The distance between previous and current position is not honored.

Other approaches for restricting the player's movement like navigation meshes is much more reliable since they account for such scenarios.

Besides, to ensure that small objects like bullets do not pass through obstacles without effect, you normally setup a ray or line segment that represents the distance between the previous and current position. You then test if this ray intersects with an object. In this way, you always detect intersections no matter of time delta and velocity.

Closing. If there is an issue with floating point inaccuracies, a live example is required for verification.

The restrictions mentioned in https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/issues/21755#issuecomment-842570740 a more of conceptual nature and only fixable with different approaches.

review_comments:
How have you come up with a value of `0.01`? 

This value is probably way to high for small scaled scenes.

You are right, for small scaled scenes the value is way too high. We are using units in millimeters, so our scene is scaled by some factor.
Since a suitable value is dependant on the scene scale, would it be an idea to add `_epsilon` as an argument to the constructor? And what would be a proper default value?

I guess I would start with the smallest possible epsilon which is `Number.EPSILON`.

Alternatively, `fromGraphNode()` could be enhanced similar to what `ConvexHull` does. Meaning it uses the input data to compute the extends along all three axes and then uses the min/max values to compute an optimal epsilon. Such an approach is in general a good approximation.
